title: Numerical experiments with the LANCELOT package (Release A) for large-scale nonlinear optimization
contribution: Describes every algorithmic option of LANCELOT Release A and tests 21 one-change variants of a documented default on 943 CUTE instances (19803 runs), giving per-option reliability and efficiency, a list of the package's weak points with planned fixes, and separate package-specific and general computational lessons.
problem_entry: Engineering question about the authors' own package: report experiments on a sizeable collection and rank the relative merits of its algorithmic options; the rival comparison with MINOS is deferred to a separate paper (p. 5).
key_idea: One-factor-at-a-time test design: a printed default specification file plus 20 basic variants that each differ from the default in exactly one option (fdg differs in two), analysed on reliability, minor iterations (= function evaluations), cg-iterations and CPU (pp. 32-34, 39).
assumptions: f and c twice continuously differentiable; group partially separable objective, justified because any function with a continuous sparse Hessian can be written so; convergence theory cited from CGT 1988/1991 rather than re-proved; HSL-dependent options cannot be defaults for licensing reasons (pp. 8, 14, 23, 34).
proof_devices: coded failure taxonomy per variant: succ/stall/infs/mem/iters/cpu/error (p. 34)
same-answer filter: count a run only if its final value matches the best critical value within 0.001% (p. 38)
averages over problems solved by all variants plus rank histograms (ranks clustered 1-3, 4-6, ...) over problems solved by any, with disagreements traced to outlier problems (pp. 39, 45)
normalized inner-work metric: cg-iterations per minor iteration per variable, in [0,1], with its approximations stated (p. 42)
a posteriori diagnostic rerun: raising the GMPS perturbation threshold to eps^(3/4) removes the overflow failures (pp. 36-37)
experiments: 943 CUTE instances (398 problems) plus a 45-problem large subset; 21 variants; limits 1000 iterations and 18000 CPU s on DECstation 5000/200; default 92.5% success, seprc 93.1%, dfp lowest; 919 solved by at least one variant; costs in minor iterations (= evaluations), cg-iterations and CPU (pp. 27-46).
positioning: Positions LANCELOT against itself (MINOS comparison deferred to [4]); rival factorization techniques (Schnabel-Eskow vs Gill-Murray-Ponceleon-Saunders) compared head to head, with the weaker one's failure diagnosed and shown avoidable; the incomplete-factorization result is qualified by the test-set make-up (pp. 5, 36-37).
writing: Numbered conclusions after each metric (13, 6, 9, 12 points), graded hedging ('perhaps surprisingly', 'admittedly marginal'), final conclusions split into package-specific and general lessons, and a closing request for user feedback (pp. 35-50).
limits_future: Weak points listed from detailed runs: slacks inflate problems with many inequalities (fix [14]), no special handling of linear or network constraints, disappointing GCP active-set prediction (barrier [15]); options to remove (l2 norm, diagonal, DFP); test set mostly well scaled; CPU measured without compiler optimization (pp. 34-35, 45, 49-50).

method_links.note: Testing twin of the LANCELOT book; theory cited at each algorithmic step; full data in companion report [16] (S103).
Public collection (CUTE, 943 instances), per-option results for 21 variants with coded failures, separately analysed large subset; minor iterations stated to equal function evaluations.
No noisy variants; second tier is large CUTE instances tagged with applications rather than live engineering problems; CPU and cg-iterations used beside evaluations.
Structure exploitation built in (group partial separability, internal variables, partitioned updates); exact second derivatives recommended whenever available, finite differences a measured fallback.

title: On the convergence of derivative-free methods for unconstrained optimization
contribution: Defines a broad class of interpolation-based derivative-free trust-region methods and proves global convergence to first-order critical points (every limit point critical) by making an explicit 'adequate geometry' condition carry the Sauer-Xu interpolation error bound.
problem_entry: Practitioner demand for minimizing expensive simulations/measurements without derivatives; sorts the user's four options (direct search, AD, finite differences, modelling f) and backs modelling with Powell's 1974 per-evaluation rate argument (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Use Newton fundamental polynomials because they carry the Sauer-Xu error formula; define adequate geometry by bounds on NFP values in a ball; cut the radius only when geometry is adequate, and certify the model in a ball proportional to ||g_k|| whenever ||g_k|| is small (pp. 7, 11, 14-15).
assumptions: f in C2 with gradient and Hessian uniformly bounded on R^n, f bounded below, model Hessians uniformly bounded; chosen to keep the analysis simple and intuitive; kappa_n admitted to serve only a theoretical purpose; no noise (pp. 6, 11).
proof_devices: NFP bound under pivot threshold by induction over pivots (Thm 1, p. 10)
existence by greedy construction: each new point maximizes the current NFP over the ball, giving NFPs bounded by 2^|Y[d]| (Thm 2, pp. 10-11)
value error bound from the Sauer-Xu path-sum bound and gradient error bound by subtracting Taylor expansions along h = delta (grad f - g_k)/||grad f - g_k|| (Thm 4, pp. 12-13)
finiteness of the certification loop by geometric shrinking of the radius: an infinite loop gives ||grad f|| <= (1/omega + kappa_eg) omega^i eps_g -> 0 (Lemma 5(iii), pp. 16-17)
first-k contradiction to bound the radius below while ||g_k|| >= kappa_g (Lemma 7, pp. 18-19)
model-to-true gradient bridge via certification in a ball of radius <= mu ||g_k|| (Lemma 10, p. 20)
all-limit-points argument bracketing subsequences t_i < l_i and bounding step lengths by function decrease (Thm 12, pp. 21-22)
experiments: none; numbers delegated to Conn-Toint 1996, and which members of the class perform best is left open (pp. 5, 22).
positioning: Section 2 is a history of Powell's derivative-free work (conjugate directions, NS01, COBYLA, quadratic interpolation) used as the paper's genealogy; mathematical debt to Sauer-Xu, Sauer, De Boor-Ron; criticality idea credited to Carter (1991) and two regions to Powell (1996) (pp. 4-5, 7, 9, 15-16).
writing: Candid hedging ('Unfortunately', 'admittedly simplistic', 'of little theoretical use'); seven numbered comments after the algorithm on what practical codes do differently; intuition sentences before and after results (pp. 10, 12, 15-17, 19).
limits_future: First order only; kappa_n impractically large; threshold pivoting does not certify adequacy; critical limit may be at infinity; future: which members perform best, extend the class, other error bounds than Sauer-Xu (pp. 11-12, 21-22).

method_links.note: All of steps 1-4 present: error bounds (Thm 4), geometric condition (adequacy), finite model improvement plus small-gradient certification (forerunner of the criticality step), proof using only adequacy; step 5 absent (no numbers).
Theorem without code or numbers; the triad is completed across papers (S019 numbers, S020 code).
Trust-region machinery (Cauchy decrease, ratio test, all-limit-points argument) transplanted into DFO; error bound imported from multivariate interpolation theory.
Known Hessian sparsity exploited by deleting monomials from the initial basis.

quotes.text: We recall here that our purpose is merely to explore a framework in which convergence theory can be discussed, and the above will serve that goal.
It is clear to the authors that much additional work remains to specify which members of the class provide the best numerical performance.

title: A derivative free optimization algorithm in practice
contribution: Presents the practical DFO interpolation trust-region code, extends it to easy and 'virtual' (pass/fail) constraints, and reports evaluation counts on CUTE and Hock-Schittkowski problems against PDS, finite-difference LANCELOT and COBYLA, plus repeated runs on a Boeing helicopter rotor problem.
problem_entry: Engineering use: expensive, derivative-free, typically noisy simulations with fewer than 100 variables (Boeing helicopter at about a minute per evaluation, so over half an hour per finite-difference gradient; engine nozzle at hours; water-network calibration) (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Quadratic-interpolation trust region with poisedness managed by Newton fundamental polynomials, radius cut only when the model is at least fully linear, minimum-Frobenius-norm underdetermined models, and constraints split into easy (in the subproblem), difficult (future) and virtual (shrink and retry on failed evaluations) (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: f in C2 although noise is expected; constraints (even virtual ones) assumed defined by smooth functions; global convergence cited to [5] with only a fully linear model required; noise robustness argued, not tested (pp. 2, 5-6, 8).
proof_devices: none (no proofs); qualitative arguments: 6 points on a line cannot support quadratic interpolation (p. 4)
noise matters only once the radius is small relative to the noise level (pp. 5-6)
equality constraints reduce the interpolation dimension (6 points instead of 15 in an affine plane of R^4) (pp. 6-7)
experiments: 26 CUTE unconstrained, 13 HS inequality and 16 HS equality problems vs PDS, LANCELOT with finite differences and COBYLA, counted in function evaluations (CPU excluded); DFO beats PDS on all 26 and COBYLA on 22 but finite-difference LANCELOT uses fewer evaluations on 16 of 26 (my tally); DFO fewest on 12/13 and 15/16 constrained; ten runs each on 11- and 31-variable helicopter instances with 15-20% failed evaluations (pp. 8-11).
positioning: Algorithm placed in the authors' lineage ([5] S013, [6] S009, [7] S019) and credited as inspired by Powell's 1994/1996 talks; rivals run as delivered; Boeing surrogate framework [3] cited only for helicopter comparisons (pp. 3, 8, 11).
writing: Engineering-audience prose: algorithm in words, no theorems, informal intuition, confident claims on noise, openly drawn flaw of its own heuristic (Figure 1), tables listed without interpretation (pp. 3-10).
limits_future: Difficult constraints out of scope; virtual-constraint heuristic may stop at a non-minimizer; local convergence only; no noisy runs; asymmetric tolerances; Table 1 not discussed; future: better virtual-constraint heuristics and difficult constraints (pp. 3, 5, 7-10).

method_links.note: Code-and-numbers member of the triad whose theorem is S013 and prototype S019.
Two tiers (CUTE/HS plus Boeing), function evaluations as the unit with CPU explicitly excluded, baselines from direct search, model-based DFO and finite differences.
Noise robustness claimed but no noisy instances; tolerances not matched across solvers.
Poisedness via NFPs picks geometry points and replacements; radius not cut before the model is fully linear.
Code tests 'fully linear', not S013's adequacy constants: a theory-code gap of the kind Workflow B's checkpoint warns about.
Boeing helicopter and nozzle problems and a university water-network user; published at an AIAA MDO symposium.
Cheap constraints handled exactly in the subproblem; equality constraints shrink the interpolation space; separability or variable importance shapes the model.

title: Gradient-based optimization of custom circuits using a static-timing formulation
contribution: Formulates static-timing transistor sizing as a smooth large-scale NLP (arrival times as variables, max replaced by inequalities), solves it with LANCELOT using adjoint time-domain sensitivities from the SPECS simulator, and demonstrates the EinsTuner prototype on ISCAS-85-derived benchmarks and real microprocessor designs.
problem_entry: Intersection of two existing approaches: dynamic tuning burdens the user with input patterns, static tuning (TILOS, convex methods) relies on crude RC delay models unsuitable for custom high-performance design; keep static path-independence with transistor-level simulation (p. 1).
key_idea: Epigraph lifting of the timing graph: every arrival time and slew becomes a variable and each max becomes one-sided inequalities, giving a smooth NLP; gradients by adjoint sensitivities per channel-connected component; LANCELOT with group partial separability, two-step updates of linear variables, aggressive trust region, failure recovery and a noise-aware stopping rule (pp. 1-5).
assumptions: Delay and slew functions C1 in widths; lumped linear fanout capacitance; saturated-ramp signals; parameterized combinational library cells with one NFET and one PFET width per CCC; only a local minimum sought because accurate simulation may destroy the convexity of simplified models; simulation data inherently noisy (pp. 2-6).
proof_devices: no theorems; formulation validated on an analytic-delay prototype with exact gradients that converged to arbitrarily small tolerances (p. 5)
adjoint sensitivity: one adjoint analysis per measurement for any number of parameters; group adjoints for linear combinations (p. 4)
KKT-based multiplier initialization at 1/n for the epigraph min-max (p. 4)
experiments: 14 combinational circuits (up to 2,796 transistors, 5,643 variables, 5,665 constraints): ISCAS-85-derived benchmarks from heuristic gain-based sizing at equal area, plus real designs at constant area and input loading; delay gains 0.92%-40.1%, constraints within 1.5 ps, at most 160 iterations, up to three days CPU; own TILOS-like tuner on accurate simulation gives 7% vs 11% and 12% vs 16%; profiling 20% simulation, 80% optimizer (pp. 5-7).
positioning: Between dynamic tuning (DELIGHT.SPICE, the authors' JiffyTune and adjoint-Lagrangian work) and static convex tuning (TILOS, Sapatnekar et al.); credits RITUAL for a similar timing-constraint formulation; criticizes rivals on model accuracy, not speed; claims uniqueness three times (pp. 1-2, 7).
writing: Formulation shown on a three-gate example before full detail; bullet lists of design choices with reasons; opinions flagged ('In our opinion'); unreconciled tension between 'simulation is expensive' (p. 5) and 80% optimizer CPU (p. 6); concrete engineering future-work list (pp. 1-7).
limits_future: Combinational parameterized cells only (custom and sequential circuits described, not implemented); long run times; noise and stopping criteria called difficult open research; Table 2 has a duplicated ifti row and a transistor-count mismatch for ioperdf; future: direct sensitivities, adjoint Lagrangian, pruning, parallel CCC simulation, adaptive device tables, two-step on arrival times, noise constraints, process corners (pp. 5-7).

method_links.note: Flagship industrial tool is gradient-based via adjoint time-domain sensitivities; structure exploited through group partial separability, two-step updates of linear variables and internal variables; supports Heuristic 1.
Co-written with IBM's EDA group, tested on real microprocessor designs, wired into the design flow by back-annotation, published at DAC.
LANCELOT, SIF and the two-step update transplanted from the authors' NLP work into circuit tuning.
Two tiers (benchmarks and real designs), but costs in iterations and CPU and the rival comparison covers only two circuits, one untabulated.
Code and numbers without a theorem; theory lives in the LANCELOT and two-step papers.
